The clinical picture suggests a pattern of self-medication for chronic headaches that resulted in acute acetaminophen-induced liver injury, which appears to have been managed.

This 37-year-old female patient presents with a progressive clinical trajectory centered on mitral valve prolapse. This 17-year-old female patient presents with a complex medical history involving Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus, eating disorders (anorexia nervosa and bulimia nervosa), secondary amenorrhea, history of refeeding syndrome, and Female Athlete Triad. Her clinical trajectory demonstrates ongoing medical instability with significant complications from both uncontrolled diabetes and severe eating disorder pathology.

This 27-year-old male software developer and endurance athlete presents with a clinical history of recurrent travel-associated illnesses and exertional complications. This 4-year-old female patient was diagnosed with oligoarticular juvenile idiopathic arthritis in January 2020, presenting with a 2-month history of intermittent fever, right knee swelling, morning limping, and difficulty walking. This 40-year-old female patient presents with a concerning clinical trajectory of recurrent pulmonary embolism over a one-year period, with three documented episodes in January 2020, July 2020, and January 2021. This 58-year-old male with a complex medical history presents with multiple active problems including chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), obstructive sleep apnea (non-compliant with CPAP), schizophrenia (chronic paranoid type), gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD), and tobacco use disorder. This 45-year-old female patient presents with a complex clinical picture centered on post-bariatric surgery complications. This 17-year-old male patient has a history of beta-thalassemia major diagnosed in January 2020, requiring chronic transfusion therapy, and secondary iron overload (transfusional hemochromatosis) diagnosed in January 2021. This 68-year-old male with a complex medical history presents to the ED on 2026-01-15 with acute left-sided neurological deficits including difficulty eating, bumping into objects on the left side, and unawareness of the left arm, consistent with acute stroke. This 32-year-old female patient presents with a concerning clinical trajectory of recurrent encephalitis-like episodes occurring approximately every 6 months. The clinical picture is highly suggestive of recurrent herpes simplex encephalitis with incomplete treatment response or treatment failure.

This 50-year-old male patient presents with a complex medical history including type 2 diabetes mellitus, gout, history of nephrolithiasis, essential hypertension, obesity, achalasia, alcohol use disorder, and folate deficiency anemia. This 24-year-old male patient has selective IgA deficiency, diagnosed following an anaphylactic reaction to plasma transfusion in January 2020, and recurrent respiratory infections as his active problem list. This 68-year-old male with a complex medical history presents with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), hypertension, and type 2 diabetes mellitus as his current active problems. This 37-year-old African American male presents with a complex clinical trajectory characterized by progressive systemic illness. His presentation included widespread dusky erythematous patches with flaccid bullae and sloughing skin on the upper trunk and face, Nikolsky sign, oropharyngeal erosions, and genital lesions. Laboratory evaluation revealed mild leukopenia and elevated liver enzymes, while skin biopsy demonstrated full-thickness epidermal necrosis with sparse lymphocytic infiltration, findings highly suggestive of Stevens-Johnson Syndrome or Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis. The patient's clinical course demonstrates a pattern of immune-mediated inflammatory responses, with the most recent severe mucocutaneous reaction likely representing a drug-induced hypersensitivity reaction in the context of his prior FSGS and participation in an anti-inflammatory clinical trial.

This 52-year-old male with hypertension and Type A aortic dissection (diagnosed January 2020) presents with recurrent symptoms suggestive of aortic pathology. He has a history of poorly controlled hypertension and is a current smoker with 30 pack-year history. In January 2020, he presented with sudden onset tearing chest pain radiating to the back, was found to have a widened mediastinum on chest X-ray, and was admitted to Cardiothoracic Surgery for definitive management of his Type A aortic dissection. In July 2020, he presented again to the ED with sudden-onset severe upper back pain radiating between his scapulae, described as tearing and worse than previous episodes. At that visit, his blood pressure was 188/92 mmHg with heart rate of 106/min, and he was noted to be diaphoretic and anxious. His active problem list currently shows hypertension, but his clinical history indicates ongoing management of Type A aortic dissection. He is currently maintained on lisinopril 20 mg and amlodipine 5 mg daily for blood pressure control. The patient's family history includes a father with abdominal aortic aneurysm and paternal grandfather with sudden cardiac death at age 50, suggesting a genetic predisposition to aortic disease.

This 69-year-old male patient presents with a complex medical history characterized by multiple thromboembolic events over the past several years. His active problem list includes hypertension, history of rheumatic fever, osteoarthritis, history of intracranial hemorrhage, Paget disease of bone, achalasia, atrial fibrillation, iliofemoral deep vein thrombosis, acute mesenteric ischemia, and acute arterial embolism of the left lower extremity. The patient's clinical trajectory demonstrates a concerning pattern of recurrent embolic events, beginning with a DVT diagnosis in 2021, followed by acute mesenteric ischemia in September 2022, acute arterial embolism of the left lower extremity in September 2023, and most recently, stroke symptoms presenting in September 2024 with right arm and face weakness. These events are likely related to his valvular atrial fibrillation, which was diagnosed in May 2020. Despite being on rivaroxaban 20 mg daily for anticoagulation, the patient continues to experience thromboembolic complications, suggesting either inadequate anticoagulation control or progression of underlying cardiovascular disease. The patient is currently managed with lisinopril, metoprolol, and ibuprofen for osteoarthritis, along with rivaroxaban. His family history includes atrial fibrillation and ischemic stroke in his father, and Paget disease in his mother.

This 78-year-old female patient presents with a complex clinical picture characterized by progressive neurological decline culminating in death. Her active problem list includes hypertension (poorly controlled), type 2 diabetes mellitus, hyperlipidemia, osteoarthritis (multijoint), and atrial fibrillation (non-valvular). Additional significant problems include mild cognitive impairment (diagnosed 2020), neurosyphilis, aortic valve stenosis, orthostatic hypotension, recurrent falls, acute subdural hematoma (2022), and cerebral amyloid angiopathy (2022). The patient's clinical trajectory demonstrates a concerning pattern of neurological deterioration: she presented in 2021 with dizziness and near-syncope, followed by increasing forgetfulness and falls in 2021, then acute confusion and agitation after a fall in March 2022 which revealed an acute subdural hematoma. In September 2022, she suffered a stroke with left parietal lobe hemorrhage presenting as sudden collapse with right-sided weakness and aphasia. Her final encounter in March 2023 involved being found unresponsive at home, with imaging showing significant right cerebral hemisphere edema consistent with cerebral amyloid angiopathy, leading to herniation and death within two hours. The patient was on multiple medications including lisinopril, metoprolol, metformin, atorvastatin, and donepezil for her various chronic conditions.

This 30-year-old female patient presents with a history of carpal tunnel syndrome (diagnosed January 2020) and gestational hypertension. Her carpal tunnel syndrome was characterized by 6-week history of numbness and tingling in the right hand affecting the thumb, index, and middle fingers, worse at night, with positive Tinel's and Phalen's signs on physical examination. She was diagnosed with gestational hypertension during her current pregnancy, which has been mild without proteinuria and managed with diet modification. In January 2022, she presented to the emergency department at term gestation with regular uterine contractions and lower back pain. Her blood pressure was 138/88 mmHg, and fetal heart tones were 140-142 bpm. The fetal fibronectin test was positive, and transvaginal ultrasound showed a cervical length of 25 mm with no funnelling, indicating a shortened cervix. Her previous pregnancy was uncomplicated with full-term vaginal delivery. Family history is notable for maternal preeclampsia and precipitous labor. She takes prenatal vitamins daily and has no known allergies. The clinical trajectory shows progression from carpal tunnel diagnosis in 2020 to current pregnancy complicated by gestational hypertension and signs of labor at term with cervical shortening.

This 34-year-old female patient has a documented active problem of upper airway cough syndrome (postnasal drip syndrome) diagnosed on January 15, 2020, following an upper respiratory tract infection. Her initial presentation involved persistent cough for 3 weeks with postnasal drip symptoms, but lung examination was unremarkable with no wheezes or rales. On October 15, 2020, she returned to Endocrinology with neck pain, throat fullness, low-grade fever, malaise, palpitations, and intermittent sweating. Physical examination revealed a tender, enlarged thyroid gland without nodularity. Laboratory evaluation demonstrated significant hyperthyroidism with suppressed TSH (<0.01 mIU/L) and elevated free thyroxine (2.5 ng/dL). Inflammatory markers were also elevated, with ESR at 70 mm/hr and CRP at 8 mg/L, suggesting an inflammatory thyroid process such as subacute thyroiditis. The patient has no medications, no significant allergies, and no other significant medical history. Her clinical trajectory shows progression from a respiratory infection to thyroid dysfunction with inflammatory features.

This 5-year-old male presents with a complex medical history including tuberous sclerosis complex, fetal alcohol syndrome, chronic granulomatous disease, reactive attachment disorder, and recurrent acute otitis media. The patient's clinical trajectory demonstrates a pattern of recurrent infections consistent with chronic granulomatous disease, including multiple skin abscesses requiring incision and drainage, recurrent pneumonia, and repeated gram-negative bacteremia (Serratia marcescens) requiring prophylactic trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. In 2021, he underwent bilateral myringotomy with tympanostomy tube placement for recurrent otitis media with tympanic membrane perforation. The most recent evaluation in July 2027 reveals significant endocrine concerns with growth plateau, delayed pubertal development, absent secondary sexual characteristics, and decreased DHEA-S and 17-hydroxy-pregnenolone levels. Physical examination demonstrates underdeveloped external genitalia with small penis, bilateral undescended testes, no pubic or axillary hair, and elevated blood pressure of 138/88 mm Hg. The patient is currently maintained on hydrocortisone, fludrocortisone, itraconazole, levetiracetam, and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for prophylaxis. His active problem list in the system currently lists only recurrent acute otitis media, though his comprehensive medical history includes multiple chronic conditions requiring ongoing multidisciplinary management.

This 22-year-old male U.S. Army Infantryman has experienced three major traumatic events over the past year. On 2020-01-15, he was shot in the abdomen with significant blood loss, leading to a diagnosis of traumatic hemorrhagic shock with acute coagulopathy. Six months later on 2020-07-15, he was found submerged in a lake unconscious with GCS 8, developing refractory hypoxemia in ARDS with bilateral diffuse infiltrates on imaging. Most recently on 2021-03-15, he presented after a high-speed motor vehicle collision with severe pelvic pain and difficulty breathing. Current examination reveals hemodynamic instability with BP 100/60, tachycardia (HR 110), tachypnea (RR 28), and hypoxemia (O2 sat 89% on room air, PaO2 60 mmHg). Physical exam demonstrates an unstable pelvis, bilateral lung crackles, and a petechial rash on the chest and axillae. The patient takes no medications and has no known allergies. Despite the documented active problems of traumatic hemorrhagic shock with acute coagulopathy and refractory hypoxemia in ARDS, the current problem list shows no active problems, suggesting these conditions may be chronic or managed. The clinical trajectory reflects a pattern of severe trauma with persistent respiratory compromise and coagulopathic sequelae.

This 55-year-old male patient presents with a complex medical history including hypertension, seropositive rheumatoid arthritis, paroxysmal atrial fibrillation, history of ventricular tachycardia, seasonal allergic rhinitis, and history of procainamide-induced systemic lupus erythematosus. The patient's most recent encounter in July 2026 was an inpatient admission to Pulmonology for progressive shortness of breath and dry cough developing over 2 weeks, with physical exam revealing end-inspiratory crackles at lung bases and chest x-ray showing bilateral reticular opacities. Prior to this, in September 2024, the patient presented to the ED with acute left calf swelling and pain, which was confirmed as acute deep vein thrombosis with an INR of 3.1 on warfarin therapy. The patient also has a history of right quadriceps tendon rupture diagnosed in September 2022 after a fall from a ladder. Current medications include warfarin, lisinopril, amlodipine, methotrexate, prednisone, propranolol, and hydrochlorothiazide. The patient has no known drug allergies and has a family history of rheumatoid arthritis, hypertension, atrial fibrillation, and coronary artery disease. The clinical trajectory demonstrates chronic management of autoimmune and cardiovascular conditions with recent acute presentations of pulmonary symptoms and venous thromboembolism.

This patient is a male with a complex congenital condition characterized by severe combined immunodeficiency (MHC Class II deficiency/Bare Lymphocyte Syndrome), confirmed by flow cytometry demonstrating markedly reduced HLA-DR expression on lymphocytes. The active problem list includes repaired cleft lip and palate, global developmental delay, failure to thrive, and chronic hypotonia. Additional diagnoses in the medical history include Down syndrome, congenital toxoplasmosis, congenital cytomegalovirus infection, Tetralogy of Fallot, Pompe disease (Glycogen Storage Disease Type II), iron deficiency anemia, and DiGeorge syndrome. The patient's clinical trajectory shows recurrent infections including recent Pneumocystis pneumonia requiring hospitalization in 2022, with the most recent ED visit in July 2023 for high fever, difficulty breathing, and severe wet cough consistent with pneumonia. Laboratory findings demonstrate persistent iron deficiency anemia with hemoglobin 9.2 g/dL and microcytic indices, while immunologic workup reveals decreased CD3+ lymphocytes. The patient is on multiple medications including trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for PCP prophylaxis, alglucosidase alfa for Pompe disease, digoxin and furosemide for cardiac function, and iron supplementation. Family history is notable for parental consanguinity, advanced maternal age, maternal infections during pregnancy, and a deceased sibling with similar presentation, suggesting a genetic etiology.

This 70-year-old male with a complex medical history has an active problem list including hypertension, hyperlipidemia, coronary artery disease (stable angina), and giant cell arteritis. He is on chronic immunosuppression with prednisone 10 mg daily for GCA, along with cardiovascular medications including aspirin, atorvastatin, lisinopril, and amlodipine. His clinical trajectory reveals progressive vascular complications over time, including cholesterol embolism diagnosed in March 2021 (evidenced by livedo reticularis, retinal emboli, and renal dysfunction), acute mesenteric ischemia in July 2022, and intestinal obstruction in January 2022. The most recent encounter in January 2023 was an ICU admission for suspected aortic dissection, presenting with tearing chest pain radiating to the back and a widened mediastinum on chest X-ray. Additional chronic conditions include recurrent benign prostatic hyperplasia and arteriovenous fistula. The patient's clinical course demonstrates a pattern of vascular complications likely related to his GCA and its treatment, with recent concern for aortic pathology requiring urgent evaluation.

This 27-year-old female patient presents with a progressive clinical course consistent with Hodgkin lymphoma, confirmed by biopsy demonstrating Reed-Sternberg cells. Her initial presentation on January 15, 2020, involved painless cervical lymphadenopathy, intermittent fevers, night sweats, and 5 kg weight loss over 2 months. Laboratory evaluation revealed elevated ESR (50 mm/hr) and mediastinal widening on chest X-ray. By February 15, 2020, she was evaluated by Hematology & Oncology where supraclavicular lymph node biopsy confirmed the diagnosis of Hodgkin lymphoma. The patient has a significant family history with a paternal cousin diagnosed with Hodgkin lymphoma at age 26. By April 15, 2020, she presented to the Emergency Department with worsening symptoms including shortness of breath, persistent cough exacerbated by lying down, severe generalized pruritus triggered by alcohol consumption, and ongoing B-symptoms. Physical examination revealed palpable non-tender lymph nodes in cervical and axillary regions with decreased breath sounds in the right upper lung field. Laboratory findings demonstrated elevated LDH (350 U/L), leukocytosis (WBC 12,000/uL), and eosinophilia (10%). Chest radiograph confirmed a mediastinal mass. The patient currently has no active medications and is NKDA. Her clinical trajectory shows disease progression from initial lymphadenopathy to respiratory compromise with mediastinal involvement, indicating advanced disease requiring urgent oncologic intervention.

The patient is a 26-year-old female with a history of hyperemesis gravidarum diagnosed during pregnancy in January 2020, characterized by persistent vomiting, ketonuria, and significant weight loss. She presented to the emergency department on January 15, 2021, with acute onset of severe right flank pain radiating to the right groin, associated with right costovertebral angle tenderness and microscopic hematuria without evidence of infection. The clinical presentation is highly suggestive of nephrolithiasis (kidney stone), which is supported by her family history of recurrent calcium oxalate nephrolithiasis in her maternal uncle. Her active problem list currently includes hyperemesis gravidarum, though this was diagnosed during her 2020 pregnancy. The patient takes only prenatal vitamins with iron and has no known drug allergies. Her clinical trajectory demonstrates a transition from pregnancy-related hyperemesis gravidarum to a new urologic presentation of likely nephrolithiasis one year later, warranting further evaluation for stone passage or intervention.

This 1-year-old male patient with Hispanic ethnicity presents with a complex multisystem genetic disorder characterized by six active problems: X-linked immunodeficiency (Hyper-IgM syndrome), Glycogen storage disease type I (von Gierke disease), Mucolipidosis type II (I-cell disease), global developmental delay with axial hypotonia, severe failure to thrive, and oropharyngeal dysphagia with aspiration risk. The patient has a significant congenital history including Hirschsprung disease (treated with Soave pull-through), galactosemia, ventricular septard defect (treated with cardiac catheterization), and neonatal sepsis. His clinical trajectory demonstrates progressive neurological decline, with the most recent encounter in July 2021 revealing worsening muscle weakness, inability to sit unsupported, and feeding deterioration. Physical examination findings include hypotonia, poor head control, hepatomegaly, coarse facial features, gingival hypertrophy, joint contractures, dysostosis multiplex, optic atrophy, and extensor plantar responses. Laboratory studies consistently demonstrate metabolic derangements including elevated lactate, uric acid, cholesterol, and triglycerides, along with metabolic acidosis. Immunologically, the patient has elevated IgM with low IgA and IgG, and absent CD40 ligand expression on activated T cells, confirming Hyper-IgM syndrome. The patient requires comprehensive management including IVIG 400 mg/kg every 4 weeks, uncooked cornstarch for glycogen storage disease, levetiracetam for seizure control, and gastrostomy tube feeding with galactose-free formula. His family history is notable for consanguineous parents, a maternal uncle who died in infancy from severe infections, and a sibling who died at age 2 from an undiagnosed metabolic illness.

This 3-year-old male patient presents with a complex medical history characterized by Von Hippel-Lindau syndrome and multiple congenital and neonatal complications. The active problem list includes laryngomalacia, congenital toxoplasmosis on chronic antimicrobial therapy (pyrimethamine, sulfadiazine, and folinic acid), severe unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia with acute bilirubin encephalopathy, cerebellar hemangioblastoma, and a ventriculoperitoneal shunt for hydrocephalus management. The patient's clinical trajectory began in early infancy with neonatal tetanus, late-onset Group B Streptococcal meningitis, and pertussis, followed by the diagnosis of congenital toxoplasmosis and hydrocephalus in January 2020. In January 2022, the patient was hospitalized for rapidly increasing head size, vomiting, and upward gaze difficulty, with MRI confirming an enhancing fourth ventricular mass consistent with cerebellar hemangioblastoma related to his VHL syndrome. The most recent ED visit in January 2023 for irritability, forceful vomiting, and excessive sleepiness revealed dilated lateral ventricles on ultrasound, suggesting possible shunt malfunction or progression of hydrocephalus. The patient remains on lifelong antimicrobial therapy for toxoplasmosis and requires ongoing neurosurgical management for his VP shunt and VHL-associated manifestations.

This 27-year-old female patient presents with a complex medical history characterized by chronic heavy menstrual bleeding (menorrhagia) since menarche, restrictive eating behavior with frequent meal skipping, and recurrent upper respiratory tract infections. Her clinical trajectory reveals progressive hematologic complications, beginning with iron deficiency anemia diagnosed in January 2020 (hemoglobin 8.2 g/dL, MCV 72 fL), followed by acute intermittent porphyria diagnosed in November 2020, likely precipitated by ibuprofen use for menstrual cramps. In November 2021, she was hospitalized for fatigue and dark urine, with laboratory evidence of hemolysis including elevated reticulocytes (8%), elevated indirect bilirubin (3.2 mg/dL), elevated LDH, and undetectable haptoglobin, leading to a diagnosis of autoimmune hemolytic anemia. The most recent encounter in November 2022 involved an ED presentation for sudden-onset right facial weakness, consistent with Bell's palsy, with no vesicular lesions or hearing changes. Family history is significant for acute intermittent porphyria (maternal grandmother), systemic lupus erythematosus (mother), and Bell's palsy (paternal aunt), suggesting a genetic predisposition to autoimmune and metabolic disorders. Current medications include sporadically taken multivitamin with iron and ibuprofen for menstrual cramps. The patient's clinical course demonstrates interrelated hematologic, metabolic, and autoimmune conditions requiring ongoing management.

This 70-year-old male patient presents with a complex clinical picture characterized by multiple cardiovascular and neurological comorbidities. His active problem list includes hypertension, Type 2 diabetes mellitus, hyperlipidemia, and degenerative conduction system disease. Additional diagnoses from his medical history include presbycusis, Mobitz type I atrioventricular block, lacunar stroke (2024), and Weber syndrome (2026). The patient's clinical trajectory demonstrates progressive neurological decline with recurrent stroke events, beginning with a lacunar infarct in 2024 presenting as right-sided numbness, followed by Weber syndrome in 2026 manifesting as midbrain infarction with contralateral weakness and cranial nerve deficits. Recent encounters in 2027 and 2028 show continued neurological deterioration with episodes of sudden weakness and double vision, culminating in ICU admission for right eye "down and out" positioning with left-sided hemiparesis. The patient is managed on a comprehensive medication regimen including metformin, dual antihypertensives (lisinopril and amlodipine), atorvastatin, and aspirin for secondary stroke prevention. Family history reveals significant cardiovascular risk factors with father's ischemic stroke, mother's diabetes and hypertension, and brother's myocardial infarction. The patient is a former smoker who quit 12 years ago and maintains social alcohol use.

This 23-year-old male patient presents with a clinical trajectory centered on hyperzincemia and its complications. He was initially diagnosed with hyperzincemia on January 15, 2020, during an outpatient visit where elevated triglycerides were identified. The patient has been taking zinc gluconate supplement 50 mg daily and multivitamin since that time. On July 15, 2020, he presented to the emergency department with recurrent episodes of severe sharp upper abdominal pain radiating to the back, accompanied by nausea and vomiting, symptoms consistent with acute pancreatitis. Laboratory evaluation revealed markedly elevated triglyceride levels at 2000 mg/dL, amylase activity of 2000 U/L, and lipase activity of 1800 U/L, confirming pancreatitis. Imaging ruled out gallstones or biliary tract obstruction as the cause. Physical examination demonstrated epigastric tenderness without rebound or guarding. The patient has no known drug allergies and reports no smoking history with only social alcohol use. Family history is notable for his father's hospitalization for pancreatitis approximately 5 years ago. The current active problem is hyperzincemia, which appears to have precipitated severe hypertriglyceridemia and subsequent acute pancreatitis. The clinical course suggests that zinc supplementation may be contributing to the hyperzincemia, which in turn has led to metabolic derangements causing pancreatitis.

This 24-year-old female patient has three active chronic conditions: migraine without aura, familial hypercholesterolemia, and latent tuberculosis infection. Her medical history includes statin-induced hepatotoxicity diagnosed in January 2020, which was evidenced by elevated AST (70 U/L) and ALT (85 U/L) at that time. In April 2020, she presented with dystonia characterized by involuntary sustained upward gaze and neck extension, diagnosed as secondary dystonia due to an intracranial lesion. The most recent significant event occurred in January 2021 when she presented to the emergency department with painful oral ulcers, fever, and a rapidly progressing rash. Physical examination revealed diffuse erythematous macules with dusky centers, flaccid bullae, positive Nikolsky sign, and mucosal involvement in the oral and genital areas. Skin biopsy demonstrated keratinocyte apoptosis with full-thickness epidermal necrosis, findings consistent with Stevens-Johnson syndrome or toxic epidermal necrolysis. She has a documented allergy to sulfamethoxazole-trimethoprim due to Stevens-Johnson syndrome. Current medications include sumatriptan for migraines, atorvastatin for hypercholesterolemia, and isoniazid with pyridoxine for latent tuberculosis infection. The patient's clinical trajectory reflects a complex history of medication-related adverse events and neurological complications, with the most recent severe cutaneous reaction raising concerns about potential drug hypersensitivity.

This 25-year-old female patient presents with a history of recurrent bacterial vaginosis, diagnosed twice in 2020 (January and July), characterized by thin, malodorous vaginal discharge with a fishy odor, elevated vaginal pH of 5.5, and positive KOH whiff test with clue cells on wet mount. Her most recent encounter in January 2021 at the emergency department involved a 3-day history of sore throat, fever (peaking at 38.9°C), and lower abdominal pain, which she attributed to unprotected oral sex with a new partner. Physical examination revealed an erythematous throat without exudates, bilateral lower abdominal quadrant tenderness, and mucopurulent cervical discharge, raising concern for a sexually transmitted infection. Laboratory evaluation showed an unremarkable urinalysis, negative rapid strep test, and nucleic acid amplification testing was performed on both pharyngeal and cervical samples. The patient is sexually active with multiple partners and inconsistently uses barrier protection, which may contribute to her recurrent infections. She has no current active problems listed, no medications, and no known drug allergies. Past surgical history includes tonsillectomy at age 8 and wisdom teeth extraction at age 20. Family history is notable for maternal hypertension and paternal type 2 diabetes mellitus.

This 25-year-old male construction laborer presents with a complex clinical history spanning three major acute events over a 2-year period. His initial encounter in January 2020 involved stimulant intoxication, characterized by agitation, rapid speech, profuse sweating, hyperthermia (38.9°C), tachycardia (130/min), and dilated pupils, with family history of alcohol use disorder and bipolar disorder. In July 2020, he was admitted to Orthopedic Surgery for acute osteomyelitis of the right foot secondary to Pseudomonas aeruginosa infection following a nail puncture injury, with elevated inflammatory markers (WBC 12,000/uL, ESR 45 mm/hr, CRP 25 mg/L). The most recent and most severe encounter occurred in September 2021 when he was admitted to the ICU for second and third-degree burns covering 40% of total body surface area from a house fire with inhalational injury requiring intubation. At that time, his PMH listed both stimulant intoxication and acute osteomyelitis as active problems, with laboratory findings showing elevated glucose (180 mg/dL), insulin, and cortisol consistent with stress response. The patient currently has no active problems in the system, no medications, and is NKDA. His clinical trajectory demonstrates a pattern of acute medical events with the most recent being a severe traumatic burn injury requiring critical care.

This 32-year-old Filipino male has a documented active problem of tuberculosis, diagnosed on 2020-01-15. The patient presents with a concerning clinical trajectory of recurrent respiratory symptoms over 1.5 years, with three emergency department visits. His initial presentation in January 2020 involved productive cough, night sweats, and 5-pound weight loss, with chest X-ray showing a right apical infiltrate. By July 2020, symptoms had progressed to include 5kg weight loss, and imaging revealed a right apical infiltrate with cavitation. The most recent encounter in July 2021 demonstrated persistent fever (38.5°C), non-productive cough, and sharp pleuritic chest pain, with chest X-ray showing right upper lobe infiltrate and hilar lymphadenopathy, plus a positive tuberculin skin test (15mm induration) and elevated ESR (55 mm/hr). The patient is a recent immigrant from a high TB prevalence country with no vaccinations or medical care since arrival, and works at a homeless shelter. Despite the 2020 TB diagnosis, the patient continues to present with active symptoms suggestive of ongoing or recurrent tuberculosis disease, indicating possible treatment failure, non-adherence, or reinfection.

This 32-year-old female patient presents with two active problems: seasonal allergic rhinitis and history of preterm labor. Her clinical trajectory reveals a pattern of recurrent obstetric complications, with preterm labor occurring at 32 weeks gestation in January 2020 and again at 34 weeks gestation in September 2021, both requiring inpatient obstetric care. In September 2020, she experienced high-altitude pulmonary edema after hiking to 12,000 feet in the Rocky Mountains, presenting with hypoxemia (86% on room air), bilateral crackles, and alveolar infiltrates on chest X-ray. She was diagnosed with respiratory distress syndrome in January 2020 following her first preterm labor event. Family history is notable for maternal aunt with high-altitude pulmonary edema susceptibility, suggesting a potential genetic predisposition. The patient is a never-smoker with social alcohol use, takes levocetirizine for seasonal allergies, and has allergies to latex and penicillin. Her current clinical picture reflects a complex history of obstetric complications and respiratory vulnerability, particularly to high-altitude exposure.

This 51-year-old male patient presents with a complex clinical trajectory involving chronic medical conditions and a recent hematologic malignancy. His active problem list includes essential hypertension, hyperlipidemia, chronic mechanical low back pain, seasonal allergic rhinitis, and arsenic toxicity diagnosed in January 2020. The patient's occupational history as a construction carpenter handling pressure-treated lumber is significant, as he was exposed to arsenic-containing materials. In January 2020, he presented with progressive neuropathy (glove-and-stocking sensory loss), skin changes (hyperpigmented/hypopigmented macules, hyperkeratotic lesions), and gastrointestinal symptoms, with laboratory findings showing anemia, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, and elevated liver enzymes. By January 2022, his condition progressed to severe pancytopenia (WBC 2,000/µL, hemoglobin 10.2 g/dL, platelets 80,000/µL) with splenomegaly on physical examination. The critical finding of abnormal cells staining positive for tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase (TRAP) is diagnostic for Hairy Cell Leukemia, a rare B-cell neoplasm. The clinical trajectory suggests that chronic arsenic exposure may have contributed to his initial toxicity symptoms, but the development of Hairy Cell Leukemia represents a distinct hematologic malignancy requiring oncologic management. The patient remains on medications for hypertension (amlodipine), hyperlipidemia (rosuvastatin), and takes acetaminophen and fluticasone for pain and allergic rhinitis respectively.

This 3-year-old male patient has a complex medical history characterized by transfusion-dependent anemia, secondary iron overload, and functional asplenia. He was diagnosed with beta-thalassemia in 2020 and vitamin A deficiency in 2020, followed by acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) diagnosis in 2022 based on bone marrow biopsy showing blast cells. His clinical trajectory has been marked by recurrent complications including a transfusion-associated circulatory overload event in July 2024 following packed red blood cell transfusion for vaso-occlusive crisis, evidenced by pulmonary edema on chest X-ray. The most recent encounter in January 2026 presents a critical clinical picture with high-grade fever (39.2°C), lethargy, anuria for 12 hours, hypotension (70/40 mmHg), tachycardia (160 bpm), and acute kidney injury (creatinine 2.1 mg/dL). Laboratory findings demonstrate severe anemia (hemoglobin 6 g/dL), leukocytosis (WBC 23,000/mm³), and thrombocytopenia (platelets 55,000/mm³), with pending blood culture results. The patient's functional asplenia places him at increased risk for severe infections from encapsulated organisms, and his current presentation is highly concerning for septic shock. He is maintained on a comprehensive medication regimen including 6-mercaptopurine for ALL maintenance, deferasirox for iron chelation, penicillin VK for infection prophylaxis, and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. His clinical course reflects the challenges of managing multiple chronic hematologic conditions with significant risk for infection and transfusion-related complications.

This 22-year-old male patient presents with a complex clinical picture characterized by recurrent high-speed motor vehicle collisions resulting in multiple traumatic injuries. His current active problem list includes attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (combined type), tobacco use disorder (moderate), alcohol use disorder (mild), and seasonal allergic rhinitis. The patient's clinical trajectory reveals a concerning pattern of repeated trauma since 2020, with documented injuries including avascular necrosis of the femoral head (2020), cervical vertebral fracture (2021), extraperitoneal bladder rupture (2022), diffuse axonal injury (2023), and most recently, a closed displaced right femur fracture complicated by acute dyspnea and confusion (2024). The 2024 hospitalization revealed fat embolism syndrome, evidenced by hypoxemia (PaO2 60 mmHg), bilateral diffuse pulmonary infiltrates on chest X-ray, tachypnea, tachycardia, and a petechial rash. Social history indicates current smoking (0.5 pack/day for 4 years), heavy episodic alcohol use with intoxication at the time of accidents, and employment as a construction laborer. The patient is currently maintained on amphetamine/dextroamphetamine for ADHD, cetirizine for allergies, and albuterol inhaler PRN. This patient requires comprehensive, multidisciplinary care addressing his substance use disorders, behavioral health needs, and ongoing risk for recurrent trauma.

This 30-year-old female patient has a history of two pregnancy-related dermatologic and hepatic conditions. In January 2020, at 35 weeks gestation, she presented with an itchy rash on her abdomen that was diagnosed as polymorphic eruption of pregnancy (pruritic urticarial papules and plaques of pregnancy), characterized by erythematous urticarial papules and plaques within striae with umbilicus spared. In September 2021, she was admitted as an inpatient with a 2-week history of severe pruritus affecting the palms and soles without associated rash, which is clinically suggestive of intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy. Laboratory evaluation at that time revealed elevated total bile acids (15 µmol/L) and mildly elevated liver enzymes (ALT 45 U/L, AST 50 U/L), supporting the diagnosis of cholestasis. The patient has no current active problems listed, suggesting she has likely delivered or the pregnancy-related conditions have resolved. Her family history is notable for a maternal aunt with acute fatty liver of pregnancy and a mother with atopic dermatitis, which may represent a predisposition to pregnancy-related dermatologic and hepatic disorders. She takes only prenatal vitamins and has no known drug allergies.

This 33-year-old male patient presents with a history of two emergency department encounters related to left upper extremity trauma. The first encounter on 2020-01-15 involved a fall while jogging that resulted in a fracture of the left humeral shaft, which was treated with open reduction and internal fixation (ORIF). The patient was diagnosed with a radial nerve injury at that time. On 2021-07-15, the patient returned to the ED after falling from a ladder while working as a roofer, presenting with sharp pain in the upper left arm. Imaging confirmed the diagnosis, and physical examination revealed significant swelling, bruising, deformity over the midportion of the left humerus, and inability to lift or extend the left wrist or fingers, with decreased sensation over the dorsal aspect of the left hand and thumb. The patient's active problem list in the system is currently empty, though clinical notes document a persistent radial nerve injury from the 2020 fracture. The patient takes no medications, has no known drug allergies, and has a social history of never smoking with social alcohol use. Family history includes hypertension in the father and type 2 diabetes in the mother. The clinical trajectory demonstrates a pattern of left arm trauma with persistent radial nerve injury, and the patient's occupation as a roofer may place him at ongoing risk for similar injuries.

This infant female patient presents with multiple cherry hemangiomas, which are benign vascular birthmarks that have been present since birth or early infancy. The clinical trajectory shows progressive evaluation of three distinct lesions: a 5 cm left cheek lesion noted in January 2020, an asymptomatic abdominal lesion enlarging since birth evaluated in April 2020, and a scalp lesion that grew from pea-sized to 2 cm by October 2020. All lesions are characterized as well-demarcated, warm to the touch, and non-tender, with the scalp lesion notably darkening when the infant cries. The patient's active problem list currently includes only cherry hemangioma, diagnosed on 2020-01-15. Family history is significant for vascular birthmarks, including a maternal first cousin with infantile hemangioma, paternal grandmother with multiple cherry angiomas, and mother with benign vascular birthmarks. The infant is otherwise healthy, meeting all developmental milestones, with normal vital signs and no other medical concerns. Current medications include Vitamin D3 supplementation and polyethylene glycol for constipation management. The clinical course demonstrates stable, benign progression of multiple cherry hemangiomas without complications or need for intervention.

This 45-year-old female patient presents with a complex clinical picture centered on paroxysmal hypertension and pheochromocytoma, likely in the context of multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2A (MEN 2A) syndrome. Her clinical trajectory began in January 2020 when she presented to Cardiology with episodic palpitations, pounding headaches, and flushing, with orthostatic hypertension (120/76 sitting to 198/102 standing) and elevated plasma metanephrines. By July 2020, during an Endocrinology visit for a palpable neck mass and diarrhea, she was diagnosed with pheochromocytoma, and laboratory evaluation revealed elevated serum calcitonin (500 pg/mL) and CEA (10 ng/mL) with a thyroid nodule, suggesting concurrent medullary thyroid carcinoma.
